headline: Two pandas flew FedEx to Atlanta. They stay 10 years.
summary: Ping Ping and Fu Shuang left Chengdu early Sunday on a Boeing 777 FedEx calls the Panda Express and landed in Atlanta that morning. Both were born in 2020. Zoo Atlanta holds them on a 10-year loan, its first pandas since 2024. Xi Jinping announced the loan Thursday at his summit with Trump. The pair sits a month in quarantine first.

cover_question.q: Why does China lend its pandas?

cover_answer: To say it wants to be friends. It can take them back.
table_question: If you lend something for 10 years, is it still yours?

5-7.script: Two pandas flew from China to Atlanta this morning on a big plane with no other passengers. Ping Ping has dark circles round his eyes and Fu Shuang has a little bump on her forehead, so you can tell them apart. They get a quiet month in their new house first, the way a new puppy hides under the bed for a week. Then the zoo opens the door.
5-7.why: Two faces and a plane. The quiet month is a puppy under a bed.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them two: the eye circles and the forehead bump, the way the keepers tell the bears apart. The quarantine month becomes a puppy under the bed, something they have seen. Expect "can we go?" Not for a month, and the zoo has not named the day.

8-12.script: China does not give pandas away. It lends them when it wants to be friendly and lets the deal run out when it is annoyed. Thursday, after three days of talks with Trump that fixed none of the big arguments, Xi announced this loan. A library book: Atlanta gets it for 10 years, and it still belongs to the library.
8-12.why: Lend, don't give. The library book carries it.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out how rules and deals fit together, so the script hands them the chain: China lends, never gives; a friendly summit produced a loan; a sour one can end it. The library book is the mechanism, borrowed and still owned. Expect "so they're not ours?" No. Ten years, then home, sooner if the governments fall out.

13-17.script: Three days of Trump and Xi fixed none of the disputes between them. The pandas were one of the few concrete results. Is a 10-year bear loan a real result or a photo op? Second: China has let panda deals lapse when relations sour. If the bears can go home when Beijing is unhappy, who is the loan for?
13-17.why: Two questions, no clean answer. Photo op first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the summit fixed nothing, and it produced something real that will live in Atlanta for a decade. The script asks whether that counts, then who a recallable gift serves. Let them argue before you weigh in. Expect "does the US do this too?" The article does not say. I don't know.

5-7.q: Can we go and see them?
5-7.a: Not for a month. They rest in quarantine first, and the zoo hasn't named the day.

8-12.q: Why does China lend its pandas?
8-12.a: It lends them to zoos it likes and lets the deals run out when it is annoyed.

8-12.q: Why can't people see them yet?
8-12.a: About a month in quarantine, in a sealed-off part of the new panda complex.

13-17.q: Why did Xi announce them himself?
13-17.a: The summit fixed no disputes. This was one of its few results.
Yes. It has let deals lapse when relations soured.
